books.audience: Data engineers, data architects, and Python developers who want to master the Apache Iceberg ecosystem using Python.
books.excerpt: The shift from managing files to managing tables is the single most important evolution in modern data architecture. For years, data engineers built "data lakes" by dumping thousands of Parquet, CSV, or JSON files into object storage buckets. They relied on directory structures and Hive metastores to make sense of this data. This approach worked until it didn't. As data volumes grew, listing files became slow, schema changes became risky, and data consistency became a nightmare. If a job failed halfway through writing a thousand files, you were left with a corrupted dataset and no easy way to roll back.

books.title: The 2026 Guide to Lakehouses, Apache Iceberg and Agentic AI
books.description: A comprehensive guide covering the convergence of lakehouse architecture, Apache Iceberg, and the rise of agentic AI systems.
toc: The Python Ecosystem for Lakehouse and AI
books.audience: Data engineers, data architects, data analysts, data scientists, analytics engineers, and AI/ML engineers who build, query, or put agentic systems on top of lakehouse data.
books.excerpt: Data has become the operational core of every modern business. From the way a retail company decides which products to stock, to how a financial institution detects fraud in real time, to how a healthcare provider personalizes treatment plans, data sits at the center of every decision. This is not a new observation, but the infrastructure that supports these decisions has undergone a fundamental transformation over the past decade. The tooling is more powerful, the architectures are more open, and the roles of the people who build and use data systems have evolved to match.

books.title: The Book on Agentic Analytics
books.description: Explores the foundations of agentic data architecture, where AI agents autonomously discover, query, and analyze data.
toc: Teaching AI the Business (The Semantic Layer)
The Interface of the Future (MCP Servers)
books.audience: Data engineers, solutions architects, and CTOs who already know SQL and Python and are being asked to make their data platform ready for AI agents.
books.excerpt: For decades, the data industry has been locked in a cycle of centralization. We built Data Warehouses to answer known questions. We built Data Lakes to store everything else. Then we built Lakehouses to try and get the best of both worlds. Yet, despite billions of dollars invested in modern data stacks, a simple question like "What was our churn rate last quarter, and how does it correlate with the new pricing model?" often takes days to answer.

books.title: Enabling Agentic Analytics with Apache Iceberg and Dremio

The MCP Server and External AI Clients
The Developer Toolkit: SDKs, APIs, and Arrow Flight
books.audience: Data engineers, data architects, analytics leaders, AI engineers, and chief data officers.
books.excerpt: This shift isn't theoretical. It's happening now. Companies are deploying AI agents that write SQL, answer business questions, and trigger automated workflows. But most of these agents are running on architectures that were never designed for them. The data is scattered across silos. The queries are too slow. The governance is too rigid or too loose. The business context that makes the difference between a useful insight and a hallucination is locked in people's heads, not in the platform.

books.title: Using AI Agents for Data Engineering and Data Analysis
books.description: A practical guide to leveraging AI agents for automating data engineering pipelines and performing intelligent data analysis.
toc: Why AI Agents Matter for Data Teams
Schema Design and DDL with Agents
Building a Semantic Layer with Agents
books.audience: Data engineers, data analysts, and analytics engineers.
books.excerpt: Data teams spend most of their time on work that follows predictable patterns. Writing DDL. Building views. Debugging a query that returns unexpected results. Classifying a column. Summarizing a table. These tasks require knowledge and judgment, but the mechanical steps are repetitive. AI coding agents can handle the mechanical part. This book teaches you how to use AI coding agents for data engineering and data analysis. Not in theory. In practice, with real tools, real SQL, and a real data platform.

books.title: The AI Engineering Handbook
books.description: A full-stack reference for building AI systems, covering LLMs, embeddings, agents, RAG, and production deployment patterns.
books.audience: AI engineers at any level who want a single reference, software engineers moving into AI engineering, full-stack developers adding AI features to applications, and technical leaders who need to understand the whole AI engineering stack.
books.excerpt: Ideal characteristics. High value and low risk: internal-facing (not customer-facing), well-defined success criteria, domain experts available for evaluation, and existing data that can power the feature. Customer support automation, internal knowledge search, and document summarization are common first projects. Avoid these as first projects. Customer-facing chatbots (too visible if quality is low), autonomous decision-making (too risky without experience), and projects requiring custom model training (too complex for a first effort).

books.title: AI-Ready Data
books.description: Designing data platforms optimized for LLMs, AI agents, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) workflows.
books.audience: Data engineers, AI and ML engineers, platform architects, and technical leaders building the data infrastructure AI systems depend on. It is about the data layer, not models, prompts, or fine-tuning.
books.excerpt: This book was written for data engineers, AI engineers, platform architects, and technical leaders who are building the data infrastructure that AI systems need to succeed. It is not a book about models, prompts, or fine-tuning. It is a book about the data layer that determines whether those models, prompts, and fine-tuning efforts produce reliable results. The premise is simple: most AI failures are data failures. A Retrieval-Augmented Generation system that retrieves stale documents produces stale answers. An AI agent that cannot discover or understand your data returns generic responses. A classification model trained on biased data produces biased predictions. Fixing any of these problems requires fixing the data, not the model.

books.title: The 2026 Guide to AI-Assisted Development
books.description: Covers prompt engineering, AI coding assistants, and agent-driven development workflows for modern software engineers.
toc: How LLMs Work (What Developers Need to Know)
Evaluation and Testing for AI-Generated Code
Security, Guardrails, and Safe Tool Use
books.audience: Working developers who want to go well beyond autocomplete, junior developers and career changers who get a structured path plus appendices on programming basics, and team leads or engineering managers who need decision frameworks for AI tooling, evaluation, security, and staffing.
books.excerpt: This book is not about AI replacing developers. It is about developers becoming more effective by using AI as a tool. Think of AI coding agents the way you think about any powerful tool: a database, a testing framework, a CI/CD pipeline. The tool does not make decisions. You make decisions. The tool executes them faster, catches some mistakes, and handles repetitive work so you can focus on the parts that require judgment.

books.title: Apache Iceberg for Agentic AI: Connecting Structured Enterprise

toc: Apache Iceberg Fundamentals for Agent Workloads

Governance and Security for Agent Data Access
books.audience: Data engineers who build Apache Iceberg pipelines but rarely think about how agents will use their tables, and AI engineers who build agent workflows but struggle to connect them to governed, structured enterprise data.
books.excerpt: The era of large language models began with documents. We taught models to read web pages, summarize PDFs, and converse in natural language based on immense corpora of unstructured text. When developers started building autonomous agents, they naturally gravitated toward the same domain. Retrieve-and-generate (RAG) pipelines became synonymous with searching a vector database of text snippets. But the most critical information in any enterprise does not live in text documents. It lives in structured tables. Revenue metrics, inventory counts, user clickstreams, and financial transactions are highly structured datasets, carefully curated and stored in data lakehouses.

books.title: The Agentic Enterprise: Deploying AI Agents Across the Modern Organization
books.description: A guide to deploying AI agents across enterprise functions, covering strategy, governance, and organizational adoption.
books.audience: Data and analytics leaders, engineering managers, IT architects, operations leaders, and compliance and governance professionals who are evaluating, building, or governing AI agents in the enterprise.
books.excerpt: Every generation of enterprise software followed the same pattern: manual process, then software-assisted process, then automated process. Payroll moved from ledger books to spreadsheets to ERP systems. Customer support moved from phone trees to ticketing systems to chatbots. Each transition reduced cost, increased speed, and shifted human effort from execution to oversight. AI agents represent the next transition. They do not just automate individual tasks. They orchestrate multi-step workflows, make decisions based on context, and interact with enterprise systems through APIs and protocols. A procurement agent does not simply fill in a purchase order template. It evaluates vendor options, checks budget thresholds, applies compliance rules, routes approvals to the right stakeholders, and generates documentation.

books.title: Constructing Context and Semantics for AI Agents
books.description: A practical guide to embeddings, knowledge graphs, memory systems, RAG, evaluation, and production agent architectures.
toc: Introduction: AI Agents and Context Overview
books.audience: AI and ML engineers building agent systems, software engineers and architects moving into AI product development, and technical leaders, product managers, and decision-makers evaluating AI agents for their organizations.
books.excerpt: A customer support bot that forgets the user's name mid-conversation. A coding assistant that ignores the project's authentication layer and writes a second one from scratch. A data analyst agent that fabricates statistics because it never received the actual dataset. These failures share a common root cause: the agent lacked the right context at the right time. Context is not a nice-to-have feature for AI agents. It is the foundation on which every useful behavior depends. An agent's ability to reason, plan, and act correctly is bounded by the information it can access during each decision. When that information is incomplete, stale, or poorly structured, the agent produces outputs that range from mildly unhelpful to dangerously wrong.

books.title: The Open Source Lakehouse: Architecting the Decoupled Analytical Foundation
books.description: Covers building a fully decoupled lakehouse using open source technologies, emphasizing modularity and vendor independence.
toc: Apache Arrow Flight: High-Performance Data Transfer
books.audience: Data engineers building pipelines, architects planning a platform migration, and technical leaders weighing the strategic implications of adopting open source data infrastructure.
books.excerpt: The modern data landscape is undergoing a profound structural transformation. For decades, organizations stored their analytical data inside proprietary systems controlled by a small number of dominant vendors. The data formats were closed. The query engines were closed. The governance policies were embedded inside opaque administrative consoles that only the vendor fully understood. Switching platforms meant migrating petabytes of data through narrow export pipelines, a process so expensive and risky that most organizations simply accepted annual price increases as the cost of doing business.

books.title: Evaluating AI Systems: Testing LLMs, RAG, and Agents
books.description: A guide to properly testing and evaluating AI systems, including benchmarking strategies for LLMs, RAG pipelines, and agents.
toc: Why Evaluation Is Different for AI
books.audience: AI and ML engineers, QA engineers, platform engineers, technical leaders, and data engineers who need systematic evaluation for AI systems. No prior evaluation experience is assumed, though basic Python, SQL, and CI/CD familiarity helps.
books.excerpt: AI systems do not work this way. Ask an LLM to summarize a quarterly earnings report and you may get a different summary each time. Both summaries might be accurate. One might emphasize revenue growth while the other leads with margin expansion. Both are correct, but they are not identical. Traditional assertion-based testing cannot handle this. This chapter establishes why AI systems require a fundamentally different approach to quality assurance, what that approach looks like at a high level, and what happens when teams skip it.

books.title: The Economics of Labor in the AI Era
books.description: Examines how the AI era is disrupting the labor market and explores paths for adaptation and the future of work.
toc: Policy Response: Safety Nets and UBI
Policy Response: Regulation and Industrial Policy
Career Strategy for the AI Era
books.audience: Knowledge workers weighing how AI affects their careers, economics students and enthusiasts, policymakers and their staffs, business leaders planning workforce strategy, and data professionals making career decisions in AI-adjacent fields.
books.excerpt: Every major technology shift produces the same argument. One side says the new technology will destroy jobs and create mass unemployment. The other side says it will create more jobs than it destroys, just as every previous technology has. Both sides cite historical evidence. Both sides are partially right. And both sides usually miss the factors that actually determine the outcome. This chapter frames the AI disruption question honestly. It examines what happened during previous technology transitions, identifies what makes AI different from those transitions, and establishes the economic frameworks this book uses to analyze what comes next.

books.title: Governing AI Systems
books.description: A guide to AI governance frameworks, covering risk management, compliance, ethics, and organizational oversight of AI systems.
toc: The EU AI Act: Practical Compliance
books.audience: AI safety and governance leaders, engineering teams implementing guardrails and compliance controls, CISOs and risk officers, legal and compliance teams, and technical leaders responsible for AI deployments that must meet regulatory requirements.
books.excerpt: AI governance is no longer a future concern. The EU AI Act's prohibitions on unacceptable-risk AI systems are already enforceable. High-risk AI system obligations take effect in August 2026. NIST's AI Risk Management Framework has become the de facto standard for voluntary compliance in the United States. ISO/IEC 42001 provides the first international standard for AI management systems. This chapter establishes why governance is an operational necessity, the cost of operating without it, and how to assess an organization's governance maturity.

books.title: Shipping AI: From Prototype to Production Systems
books.description: Covers the full lifecycle of taking AI systems from prototype to production, including deployment, scaling, and monitoring.
books.audience: AI and ML engineers, platform engineers, engineering managers, DevOps and SRE teams, and data engineers who build or run AI systems in production. It assumes software engineering fundamentals but no machine learning research background.
books.excerpt: Every AI demo lies. Not intentionally, but structurally. A prototype that answers questions correctly on a developer's laptop tells you nothing about how it will perform when 500 users hit it simultaneously, when the model returns a hallucinated answer to a customer's billing question, or when your monthly inference bill arrives at six figures. The gap between a working AI prototype and a production AI system is wider than most engineers expect. This chapter explains why that gap exists, what falls into it, and how to assess whether your system is ready to cross it.

books.title: Building Knowledge Systems for AI: Graphs, RAG, Memory, and Context
books.description: A deep dive into building robust knowledge systems for AI using knowledge graphs, RAG, memory architectures, and context management.
toc: Building Knowledge Graphs from Unstructured Data
books.audience: AI engineers designing knowledge retrieval for agents, knowledge engineers and data architects building enterprise knowledge infrastructure, search engineers moving to AI-powered retrieval, and technical leaders evaluating knowledge system architectures.
books.excerpt: A product team at a mid-size financial services company built a customer support chatbot in three days. They connected GPT-5.4 to a simple chat interface, wrote a system prompt describing the company's products, and launched it internally. The first day went well. On the second day, a customer asked about a pricing change that had been announced the previous week. The chatbot confidently quoted the old pricing. On the third day, a customer asked whether their account qualified for a recently introduced loyalty discount. The chatbot invented a discount program that did not exist.

books.title: The AI Lakehouse: Architecting Data Platforms for AI
books.description: Explores how to architect data lakehouse platforms specifically designed to serve AI and machine learning workloads.
toc: The Convergence of Data and AI
books.audience: Data platform architects, data engineers, AI and ML engineers, and technical leaders and CDOs deciding how a lakehouse should serve both analytics and AI workloads.
books.excerpt: Every organization building AI systems today faces the same architectural question: where does the data live, and how do AI workloads get to it? For most companies, the answer is messy. Analytics data sits in a data warehouse. Raw files live in a data lake. Embeddings go into a vector database. Features get computed somewhere else and served from a feature store. Training datasets are exported, transformed, and versioned in yet another system. Each of these systems has its own security model, its own governance policies, and its own operations team.

books.title: AI Application Architecture: Patterns for Building Intelligent Systems
books.description: Covers architectural patterns for building intelligent applications, from inference pipelines to multi-agent orchestration.
books.audience: AI engineers and software architects designing AI applications, backend engineers adding AI to existing systems, platform engineers building shared AI infrastructure, and technical leaders choosing architectural approaches.
books.excerpt: Building an AI application is easy. Keeping it running in production is hard. The gap between a working prototype and a production system is the same gap that software engineering has been bridging for decades: the gap between "it works on my machine" and "it works for a thousand users at 3 AM." This chapter establishes why AI systems need architectural discipline, what makes AI architecture different from traditional software architecture, and the cost of getting it wrong.

books.title: The Economics of AI: Cost, Latency, and Infrastructure Tradeoffs
books.description: Analyzes the cost structures of AI systems and how to optimize spending across compute, latency, and infrastructure.
books.audience: Engineering and platform leaders, FinOps teams, AI engineers, CTOs and VPs of Engineering, and product managers who need to make AI systems financially sustainable.
books.excerpt: AI costs work differently from traditional software costs. A web application's marginal cost per user is close to zero once the infrastructure is in place. Serve one user or one million users: the database query cost barely changes. An AI application's marginal cost scales with every request: every query consumes tokens, every token costs money, and the cost varies dramatically based on model, context size, and output length.

books.title: Alex Merced's Field Guide to Developer Relations

books.audience: Developer advocates, technical evangelists, DevRel managers, and community managers who want a structured approach to the job, plus engineers moving into advocacy and founders or marketing leaders building a DevRel function.
books.excerpt: Instead of writing code, I spent my college years at Bowling Green State University studying Popular Culture and Marketing. I ran a hobby store called The Gamers Lounge and served as the promotion director for our campus radio station. I learned early on how to organize events, build excitement around niche topics, and connect people who shared similar passions. My early technical curiosity was replaced by a deep immersion in community building.

The best way to learn AI is to practice on real but low-risk work: emails, notes, research, presentations, folders, planning, and everyday decisions. The examples in this book are designed to help you build that habit one step at a time.

books.title: The No Lock-in Apache Iceberg Lakehouse with Agentic Analytics

books.audience: Data engineers, analytics engineers, data architects, platform teams, and technical leaders evaluating Apache Iceberg, open catalogs, federated query, lakehouse migrations, or agentic analytics. It assumes comfort with data platform concepts.
books.excerpt: A data team rarely wakes up one morning and decides to build a lakehouse. The usual path is less tidy. First there is a warehouse. It answers the finance dashboard, the executive scorecard, the recurring sales report, and the board deck. It has carefully modeled tables, access controls, and enough structure that people outside the data team can trust what they see. Then the business starts collecting more data than the warehouse was designed to handle comfortably: application logs, clickstreams, partner files, IoT events, document text, audio, images, model features, and raw operational extracts that might matter someday. A data lake appears because object storage is cheap, flexible, and forgiving.

books.title: Being Productive with Google AI
books.description: A practical guide to using Google's AI ecosystem including Gemini, NotebookLM, Veo, Gemini Spark, and Jules.

books.audience: Written for Google Workspace power users, researchers and knowledge managers, developers adding Google AI to their stack, and content creators who want to turn Gemini, NotebookLM, and related tools into a real daily workflow.
books.excerpt: Every morning before I start writing, I open NotebookLM. I have a notebook with 40-something sources in it: research papers, product documentation pages, previous chapters I have written, interview transcripts, blog posts I saved months ago and never got around to reading properly. Before I sit down to write anything substantial, I ask NotebookLM a question about whatever I am working on that day. Sometimes the question is broad: "What are the most important points I have not addressed yet in my sources on this topic?" Sometimes it is narrow: "Which of my sources mentions the context window size constraint in a way that I could cite directly?" The answers take about two seconds.

books.excerpt: The question that started this book was simple: what happens when the API credits run out? I had been using proprietary AI coding services daily for months. The workflow was good. The productivity gains were real. Then I got a bill that made me think seriously about what I was actually depending on. Not the model, not the workflow, but a specific company's pricing decisions, rate limits, and uptime SLAs.

books.excerpt: The first time I ran Claude Code on a real project, I expected a capable autocomplete. What I got was something closer to a junior developer who had already read the entire codebase, remembered every decision I had made in the last three sessions, and asked clarifying questions before touching anything it was not sure about. That experience changed how I thought about working with AI tools. It stopped being a question of whether to use them and became a question of how to design the working relationship deliberately.

books.excerpt: The first time I delegated a real task to Codex and walked away from my computer, I came back to a diff that was better than what I would have written myself. That had not happened with any previous AI tool. It did not just return a suggestion for me to evaluate. It returned a result I could ship. That moment changed how I thought about agentic AI, and it changed what I thought a book about agentic AI needed to cover.

books.excerpt: Every morning before I start writing, I open Cursor. I have a local workspace directory with structured rule files, project specifications, and raw manuscript drafts. Before I write a line of prose or code, I ask Grok Chat to summarize my research inputs. Sometimes the query is broad: "What are the most important points I have not addressed yet in my outline?" Sometimes it is narrow: "Which of my research documents describes the NPU requirements in a way that I can cite directly?" The answers take about two seconds, citing the exact source files and passages.

books.excerpt: The first time Microsoft 365 Copilot summarized an entire week of email threads, identified the three things I needed to act on, and drafted the follow-up for each one, I stopped thinking of it as an assistant and started treating it as infrastructure. That shift from "useful novelty" to "load-bearing part of the workflow" is what this book is about. It does not happen automatically when you get access to Copilot. It requires understanding what each Copilot surface actually does, which data it can and cannot access, what prompt structure gets consistent results, and how to verify what you receive before you act on it.

books.excerpt: In 1970, a mathematician named Edgar Codd published a paper at IBM Research that would ultimately become one of the most consequential documents in the history of computing. The paper proposed organizing data into relations, or tables, and querying those tables using a declarative language. The idea was radical: instead of telling a computer how to retrieve data, step by procedural step, you simply described what data you wanted, and the engine figured out the mechanics on its own.

books.excerpt: Every significant shift in computing follows the same pattern. First, the early adopters build something that works but is hard to use. Then, the tooling matures, the costs drop, and suddenly an entire industry reorganizes around the new approach. We saw it with relational databases in the 1980s, with the web in the 1990s, with cloud computing in the 2010s, and we are living through it right now with two simultaneous revolutions: the open data lakehouse and artificial intelligence.

books.audience: Data engineers, analytics engineers, software developers, and technical leaders who want practical blueprints for an Apache Iceberg lakehouse, whether they are leaving a legacy cloud warehouse, adding generative AI to BI, or learning the Iceberg ecosystem.
books.excerpt: Data has gravity. The moment you place a terabyte of information into a proprietary database, it begins pulling your budget, your engineering time, and your architectural decisions toward that single vendor. Ten years ago, data engineers accepted this gravity as a law of physics. If you wanted fast, reliable SQL analytics, you paid a premium for an enterprise data warehouse. If you wanted cheap storage for unstructured files, you dumped them into a data lake. Organizations ran both systems simultaneously, building complex pipelines to shuffle data between the cheap swamp and the expensive fortress.

books.title: The Book on Apache Polaris
books.description: Building the open data lakehouse with the industry standard Iceberg REST catalog.
toc: The Lakehouse Catalog and the REST Catalog Specification
The Command Line Interface and Admin Tool
The Polaris API, Spark Client, and Evolution
books.audience: Data engineers, data architects, platform engineers, and technical leaders who design, build, or scale open data lakehouses and want to avoid catalog lock-in and understand the Iceberg REST specification.
books.excerpt: A company with forty terabytes of sales records, customer interactions, and supply chain events faces a decision that will shape its data strategy for the next decade. The data lives in object storage already, sitting in hundreds of thousands of files across S3 buckets and Azure containers. Analysts want to run SQL queries against it. Data scientists want to train models on it. The finance team wants a dashboard that updates every morning by 7 a.m. The question is not whether to store the data. The question is how to make it useful.

books.title: Reputation as Code
books.description: The companion book to branding.alexmerced.com, covering personal branding, reputation engineering, and career sovereignty for developers and tech professionals.
toc: Introduction: The Resume Is a Dead Format
The Fallacy of the Job Board Lottery
The Myth of the Overnight Authority
The Discipline of Learning in Public
Responsible AI as an Output Amplifier
Community as an Engine of Generosity
The Path to Authoring Technical Books
Staying Curious for the Long Haul
books.audience: Software engineers, data practitioners, DevRel professionals, and other technical contributors who want to be known for their expertise without becoming shallow influencers, plus career switchers who need to show credibility without an elite pedigree.
books.excerpt: On a Monday morning in early 2024, a hiring manager at a mid-sized data infrastructure company posted an open role for a developer advocate. The listing was live for four hours. When she paused the posting at noon to review incoming candidates, the applicant tracking dashboard displayed 842 submissions. Eight hundred and forty-two resumes. If she spent sixty seconds reading each submission without taking a bathroom break, drinking water, or answering an email, reviewing that single batch would require fourteen continuous hours of work. She did not have fourteen hours. She had thirty minutes between a sprint planning meeting and a customer demo.

books.title: Economic Ideas: From Beginning to Early 2026
books.description: A survey of the history of economic thought, tracing ideas from ancient civilizations through the modern AI era.
toc: Before Economics: Trade, Barter, and the First Questions About Value
Greek Foundations: Xenophon, Plato, and Aristotle on Wealth and the Good Life
Rome, Roads, and the Price of Empire
Medieval Economics: Just Price, Usury, and the Scholastics
The Islamic Golden Age: Ibn Khaldun and the Economics of Civilization
Mercantilism: Gold, Trade Wars, and the Birth of Economic Policy
Richard Cantillon: The Secret Father of Economics
Adam Smith: The Invisible Hand and the Wealth of Nations
David Ricardo: Comparative Advantage and the Logic of Trade
Thomas Malthus: Population, Poverty, and the Dismal Science
John Stuart Mill: The Liberal Reformer
Karl Marx: Capital, Exploitation, and Revolution
The Marginalist Revolution: Value Is in the Eye of the Buyer
The Methodenstreit: How Should We Do Economics?
Henry George: Progress, Poverty, and the Tax on Land
The American Institutionalists: Economics Gets Real
The Gold Standard: Monetary Orthodoxy and Its Discontents
The Austrian School: Mises, Hayek, and the Socialist Calculation Debate
John Maynard Keynes: The General Theory and the End of Laissez-Faire
The Keynesian Consensus and the Postwar Boom
The Chicago School: Milton Friedman and the Monetarist Counterrevolution
Development Economics: Why Are Some Countries Rich and Others Poor?
Public Choice Theory: When Government Fails
Game Theory: Strategy, Conflict, and Cooperation
Rational Expectations and the New Classical Revolution
Supply-Side Economics: Tax Cuts and the Laffer Curve
The Fall of Communism and Transition Economics
Behavioral Economics: When People Are Not Rational
Information Economics: When Markets Know Too Little
books.audience: General readers curious about economics, history, or political theory, including students, professionals, policymakers, and self-taught learners. No economics degree, equations, or prerequisites are needed.
books.excerpt: Economics is among the oldest and most contested fields of human inquiry. For as long as people have lived in societies, they have debated how to allocate scarce resources, organize production, distribute wealth, and design the institutional rules that govern exchange. These debates are not merely academic. They shape the policies that determine whether nations prosper or stagnate, whether individuals enjoy material comfort or endure deprivation, and whether democratic societies hold together or fracture under the weight of inequality and distrust. This book tells the story of those debates from the very beginning to the early months of 2026.

books.title: The Field Guide to Libertarianism
books.description: An accessible introduction to libertarian ideas, key debates, and the spectrum of thought within the libertarian tradition.
toc: What Is Libertarianism? Mapping the Territory
Objectivism: Ayn Rand and the Philosophy of Rational Self-Interest
Anarcho-Capitalism: Murray Rothbard and the Abolition of the State
Paleolibertarianism and Right-Libertarianism: The Conservative Turn
Libertarian Populism and the Liberty Movement Post-Ron Paul
The Expanding Tent: Libertarian Feminism, Black Libertarianism, and New Voices
Money, Banking, and the Federal Reserve
Trade and Immigration: Open Borders or Fortress Liberty?
Guns, Self-Defense, and the Second Amendment
Education: The Case Against Compulsory Schooling
Healthcare: Markets, Medicine, and the Price of Government Intervention
The Environment: Property Rights as Conservation
Criminal Justice: Victimless Crimes, Mass Incarceration, and Restorative Alternatives
Strategy Over Policy: Why Libertarianism Needs More Than Arguments
Mutual Aid: The Forgotten Libertarian Tradition
books.audience: Libertarians who want to understand the full tradition beyond their own corner of it, non-libertarians who want to know where libertarian arguments come from, and political science students looking for a readable survey.
books.excerpt: Nowadays I find myself in no particular libertarian camp. What I want, more than any policy outcome, is for people regardless of ideology to be nicer and more open to each other. Open to the human experiences we can have with other individuals and the communities we choose to enrich our lives with. Open to seeing the value of protecting the autonomy that makes those enriching experiences possible, whether through the freedom itself or through the prosperity that gives us the leisure to enjoy that freedom.

books.title: The Field Guide to Political Thought and Debates in the United States
books.description: Maps the terrain of American political thought (conservative, progressive, and libertarian) so you can understand why people across the table believe what they believe and how to talk about it.
toc: The Evolution of Conservative Thought in America
The Evolution of Progressive and Liberal Thought
The Libertarian Tradition and the Limits of the Left-Right Spectrum
Economics and the Role of Government
The Stories We Tell (and the Ones We Don't Hear)
Finding Common Ground (Without Pretending We Agree)
books.audience: Anyone who wants to understand why a family member, coworker, or neighbor who votes differently reasons the way they do, whatever their own leaning: left, right, libertarian, or unlabeled.
books.excerpt: This book will not tell you what to think. If you are looking for confirmation that your political views are correct and the other side is wrong, this is not the book for you. There are thousands of those books. They sell well. They change very few minds. This book does something harder. It maps the terrain. It traces the intellectual roots of conservatism, progressivism, and libertarianism in the United States. It examines the flashpoint issues that dominate our politics. And it presents every major argument in its strongest, most honest form, including the ones you disagree with.

books.title: The Libertarian Heart
books.description: A philosophical exploration of consent, individual peace, and the moral foundations of a free society.

books.title: Profits are Generosity, Entrepreneurship is Philanthropy
books.description: An economic philosophy book arguing that voluntary exchange and entrepreneurship are the most generous forms of social contribution.

books.title: The Semantic Rebellion
books.description: A sci-fi novel following a data engineer's journey through a rapidly changing world shaped by AI and shifting power dynamics.
toc: Proof of Concept, Proof of Value
books.audience: A techno-thriller for readers who believe transparency is a powerful force in a democracy, pitched to fans of Michael Crichton and Daniel Suarez and to anyone who has been worn down by being on call for broken systems.
books.excerpt: The phone buzzed at 2:13 in the morning. Not the gentle hum of a text message or the cheerful ping of a social media notification. This was the buzz. The angry, insistent vibration pattern that Alexjandro Olced had programmed specifically for PagerDuty alerts, the one that invaded his nervous system like a cattle prod wrapped in anxiety. He reached for the nightstand without opening his eyes, knocking over a glass of water in the process. The water spread across the wood surface and began dripping onto the carpet with the quiet patience of a system designed to ruin everything it touched.

books.title: The Emperors of A.I. Valley
books.description: A near-future thriller exploring power struggles, corporate intrigue, and moral dilemmas in an AI-dominated Silicon Valley.
books.audience: Pitched to readers of Michael Lewis and Blake Crouch, and to anyone who suspects the real story of AI is playing out behind closed doors.
books.excerpt: The oak paneling in the Hart Senate Office Building hearing room felt aggressively solid. Suae Canbote sat at the witness table and let her fingertips rest against the polished wood. She breathed strictly through her nose. The air in the room was overly conditioned and carried the faint scent of floor wax and anxious perspiration. This was the epicenter of the American political apparatus. It was also, she knew, a theater designed to intimidate those who did not understand its true function.

books.title: The Federation of Tides
books.description: An epic fantasy adventure following a narwhal on a journey seeking knowledge across oceanic civilizations.
toc: The Apprentice of the Coral Scripts
books.audience: Written for adults and mature young adult readers who like philosophical fantasy, allegory about how systems work, and stories driven by their worlds.
books.excerpt: The library breathed. It was not a metaphor. The walls of the Coral Script Archive pulsed gently with each shift of the thermal current beneath it, expanding and contracting like the ribcage of some enormous sleeping creature. Bioluminescent algae threaded through the living coral emitted a soft cerulean glow that shifted in intensity with the water's temperature, casting the vast chamber in perpetual twilight. Scrolls of pressed kelp and tablets of calcified coral lined every surface, thousands of them, organized according to a classification system so ancient that even the archivists sometimes argued about its logic.

books.title: Plastic Punk
books.description: A genre-bending novel exploring economic systems, societal structures, and individual agency in a stylized world.
toc: The Seed That Grows in Poison
The Map of What Comes Next
books.audience: Written for adults and mature young adult readers interested in economics, governance, environmental futures, and speculative fiction.
books.excerpt: The harbor of Vaelport glowed like a fever dream. Kael Doss stood at the rail of the cargo vessel Reclaimer's Profit and watched the city materialize through a haze of polymer particulate that turned the sunset into something obscene. The towers caught the dying light and amplified it. Every building in the skyline was made from compression-molded plastic, and every surface was embedded with LED filaments powered by pyro-gas running through conduits in the walls. The result was a city that burned from within, neon pinks and electric blues and acid greens bleeding into the orange sky until the boundary between architecture and atmosphere dissolved entirely.

books.title: Embers of Claim
books.description: The first book in an epic fantasy trilogy, introducing a world of competing kingdoms, ancient magic, and rising conflict.
books.audience: Adult fantasy readers who enjoy political strategy, clashing factions, ideological tension, and characters whose arcs turn on power.
books.excerpt: The hammer rang against the anvil three times before the steel gave in. Kael Astren wiped the soot from his forehead with the back of his wrist and held the iron rod up to the light streaming through the forge's single window. The metal glowed orange at the tip, fading to dull gray along the shaft where the heat had not fully penetrated. Not good enough. The color needed to be even, a consistent cherry-red from end to end, before he could begin shaping. He set it back on the coals and worked the bellows with his left hand while reaching for the tongs with his right.

books.title: Crowns and Wings
books.description: The second book in the epic fantasy trilogy, deepening the political intrigue and expanding the world's mythology.
books.audience: Adult fantasy readers who enjoy political strategy, clashing factions, ideological tension, and characters whose arcs turn on power.
books.excerpt: Two years changed everything and nothing. The kingdom of Valdren, which had been a single city and a stolen throne when Kael Astren first sat on the ugly oak chair in Valdren Hall, now stretched from the northern border marches to the southern coast of the Western Reach. Five additional territories had been absorbed since the coronation, each through the same process that had proven so effective in the first year: competent diplomacy, transparent governance terms, and the quiet gravitational pull of an administration that functioned better than anything the absorbed territories had experienced in living memory.

books.title: Thrones of Ash and Sky
books.description: The concluding volume of the trilogy, bringing the saga of kingdoms, magic, and destiny to its climax.
books.audience: Adult fantasy readers who enjoy political strategy, clashing factions, ideological tension, and characters whose arcs turn on power.
books.excerpt: The harbor at Port Tamas could hold forty ships at anchor, and on the morning the summit began, it held thirty-seven. Twelve flew the Western Empire's new device: the iron-crowned stag on a field of black. Eight flew the Federation's five-seal banner, the interlocking circles that represented the original signatory states. The remaining seventeen flew independent merchant flags, the commercial entities whose trade depended on whichever political arrangement the next days produced and who had positioned themselves in the harbor to observe, to profit, and to sell information to both sides.

books.title: Tales of Fur and Sky: Echoes of the Ages
books.description: A companion volume to the fantasy trilogy, expanding the lore with standalone tales set in the same world.
books.audience: A companion anthology of seven standalone short stories for readers returning to the world of the Thrones of Fur and Sky saga.
books.excerpt: The smell of burning cedar woke Corin before the screaming started. For a moment, he lay still in the suffocating darkness of his narrow alcove off the royal corridor. He was fifteen, the third and least favored assistant to the Master of Wardrobe, whose primary duty was ensuring the young Prince Edrin never appeared before the court with a wrinkled tunic or a scuffed boot. It was a position of proximity without power, visibility without consequence. Corin had spent the last three years melting into the tapestries, trying to be as unnoticeable as the dust motes.

books.title: Signal and Noise
books.description: A literary novel tracing a twelve-year long-distance connection between a documentary producer in Manila and a logistics manager in Indiana, and the single hour that finally tests it.
books.audience: Adults roughly 25 to 45 who like character-driven literary fiction about first love and its lasting damage, long-distance relationships, chosen family, trans identity, and co-dependency.
books.excerpt: She has not set an alarm. The alarm is the street: the tinny horn of a jeepney driver who likes to announce his displeasure with the intersection below, the drag of a metal gate being unlocked at the sari-sari across the road, a dog that has been debating something philosophical with another dog for what sounds like the past twenty minutes. She lives in Sampaloc because it is cheap and close to the university she just finished attending and because her college roommate Josie had a cousin with a vacancy on the third floor of a narrow building that smells permanently of mothballs and something faintly sweet she has decided not to investigate.

books.title: Celestial Fragments: The Duel of Souls
books.description: A contemporary fantasy in which two political rivals discover they carry the fragments of ancient beings of love and hate, continuing a conflict twelve thousand years old.
books.audience: Adults who enjoy contemporary fantasy with real-world political tension and mythological roots, and themes of identity, inclusion, and empathy versus prejudice.
books.excerpt: The girl would not stop shaking. She sat in the plastic chair with her knees drawn up, sneakers on the seat, arms wrapped around her shins. Her name was Dani. Fourteen years old. She had been coming to the Northside Youth Center for seven months, long enough for Rowan to know that she chewed her thumbnail when she was thinking and braided her hair when she was happy and pulled at the hem of her shirt when something was wrong. Today she was pulling at her hem so hard the stitching had started to give.

books.title: Adventures in Love and Flooding
books.description: A romantic action thriller about disaster capitalism, artificial intelligence, and ordinary competence. He crossed an ocean for a woman he had only ever met on a screen, and landed four days before the water came.
toc: Prologue: The Sluice Gate at Midnight
Dinner in Makati, Eyes in the Mirror
The Snare in the Server Farm
books.audience: A romantic action thriller for readers who want grounded thrillers, genuinely funny romance, and villains who fight with arithmetic rather than speeches.
books.excerpt: The call came at ten past two, which was the hour Benigno Santos had come to think of as belonging to the floodway. Nothing was ever decided at two in the morning. Things were only discovered then, and usually by him. He took the service road with his wipers on the fastest setting they had, which was not fast enough, and which had not been fast enough for four years. The truck was a white DPWH pickup with a bent antenna and a dent in the tailgate from a jeepney in Pasig that had never stopped. Rain came off the windshield in sheets rather than drops. Past the guardrail the Marikina moved in the dark like something with a shoulder.

books.title: The Last Continue
books.description: A novel about finishing things, and about what a finished life turns out to be for. A clockmaker in Manchester, Connecticut spends fifty-six years noticing that the world does not always keep time.
books.audience: A standalone novel pitched to readers of Kazuo Ishiguro, Emily St. John Mandel, and Ted Chiang.
books.excerpt: By nine that August morning Tito Mendez had the movement spread across a bath towel on the repair bench under the apple tree: mainspring barrel to one side, escapement to the other, the little forest of brass posts standing in their holes like a town he knew street by street. The clock belonged to Mrs. Gong next door. It had kept time in her kitchen for forty-five years, through two stove fires and one flood and the year her sons both left, which she mentioned every time she brought it over for service, so that by now the clock and its history arrived together, like an old married couple.

books.title: The Children of Damaris
books.description: The Worlds Between Home, Book 1 of 10. A ship mechanic, a surgical assistant, and their two children steal a damaged survey courier to escape a fascist world that has begun taking every child into state custody, with a whispering stuffed animal hidden aboard.
books.audience: Crossover young adult and adult readers who enjoy political science fiction, dystopian adventure, and family-centered space opera.
books.excerpt: The noise was three flutters to a second, soft as a moth in a jar, and it was coming from somewhere inside eleven tons of machinery that the Human Continuity Directorate had certified as sound. Aldex Oled knelt in the drive space of the courier and pressed the flat of the sounding rod against the aft coil housing. He closed his eyes. Around him the CDV Wayward ticked and settled in her berth cradle, the way any ship did when her systems were cycled down to maintenance draw, and beneath all of that ordinary settling the flutter went on. Three to a second. Not the damper packs.

books.title: A Crown of Cliffs
books.description: The Worlds Between Home, Book 2 of 10. The Oleds land on Cyradon, a canyon kingdom where every load-bearing part carries a household's name, and survive on a queen's revocable guest-oath while their asylum claim waits in court.
books.audience: Crossover young adult and adult readers who enjoy political science fiction, dystopian adventure, and family-centered space opera.
books.excerpt: The tow took nine hours, and for eight of them Aldex Oled sat in the left-hand seat of a ship he no longer had any way to fly and worked on the only problem left to him, which was the problem of a stuffed animal. The Wayward hung on two cables at the end of a Crown tug, nose down four degrees, and every twenty minutes or so the cables took up some slack and put a long shudder through her from the spine outward, and each time Aldex felt the aft coil housing answer it with a low grinding note that no housing should be able to make. She was finished.

books.title: The Price of High Ground
books.description: The Worlds Between Home, Book 3 of 10. On Vanthel, where arrival is an invoice and every charge is published, the family learns that each honest offer made to them comes with a claim on their ship.
books.audience: Crossover young adult and adult readers who enjoy political science fiction, dystopian adventure, and family-centered space opera.
books.excerpt: The berth cost four hundred and eleven a day and Aldex Oled did not find that out until the Wayward was already in it. He had been proud of the contract. That was the part he kept coming back to, afterward, in the months that followed: not that he had been cheated, because he had not been cheated, and not that anybody had lied to him, because nobody had. He had been proud.

books.title: The Common Sun
books.description: The Worlds Between Home, Book 4 of 10. Solvara's generous public system heals the family and repairs their ship for free, yet every entitlement costs them something they did not know they were holding.
books.audience: Crossover young adult and adult readers who enjoy political science fiction, dystopian adventure, and family-centered space opera.
books.excerpt: The tender came up to meet them, and that was the first thing that was wrong. Seti Oled had been aft for eleven hours with her back against the transverse and Renna Twelfth's left arm across her knees, and she felt the match before she understood it: the small correcting shove of another hull coming alongside, close, deliberate, from below. She knew what that was. She had spent three worlds learning what that was.

books.title: What the Models Cannot See
books.description: The Worlds Between Home, Book 5 of 10. The best-run world the Oleds have seen places them under a formal hold, and ten-year-old Xia's refusals become the only thing standing between careful assessors and the voice she talks to.
books.audience: Crossover young adult and adult readers who enjoy political science fiction, dystopian adventure, and family-centered space opera.
books.excerpt: They gave him the rules on the second morning, printed, on paper, which Aldex had not expected and which he understood about four days later had been a deliberate choice. "You will want to check them against what we do," said Tolvan Reike. "You cannot check a screen. A screen is whatever we set it to this morning." There were nine pages.

books.title: The Memory Garden
books.description: The Worlds Between Home, Book 6 of 10. On Varduun nothing is withheld and nothing is billed, the memory gardens keep what people say for nine hundred years, and Xia carries something that took an entire hillside without asking.
books.audience: Crossover young adult and adult readers who enjoy political science fiction, dystopian adventure, and family-centered space opera.
books.excerpt: The table was nine meters long and there were about forty people eating at it, and the intake was the same table. Rodex had worked that out by the third day and had not believed it until the ninth, which was the day they were formally received, and even then he spent the first quarter of an hour waiting for somebody to move them to a different room.

books.title: No One Commands the Tunnels
books.description: The Worlds Between Home, Book 7 of 10. Caldris runs on syndicates, chambers, and signed findings instead of offices, and a family nobody refuses finds that nobody is able to accept them either.
books.audience: Crossover young adult and adult readers who enjoy political science fiction, dystopian adventure, and family-centered space opera.
books.excerpt: The housing had come up from the west field on the back of a hauler with a note tied to it in string, and the note said that it passed the plug and ran hot anyway and that somebody at Ondrave could look at it if somebody at Ondrave had nothing better to do. That was the fourth day, and by the fourth day Aldex had stopped waiting for the rest of the process. There was no rest of the process. Work moved on this port on haulers with string on it.

books.title: Terms of Protection
books.description: The Worlds Between Home, Book 8 of 10. On the Orison Exchange, air is the currency and protection is bought from competing houses, so the Oleds end up covered on three separate books by people who all deal with them honestly.
books.audience: Crossover young adult and adult readers who enjoy political science fiction, dystopian adventure, and family-centered space opera.
books.excerpt: Ninety-two hours of the arrival allowance had run and eight were left, and Herrol Danch walked out to pad nine to say so with his hood in his hand, which was eleven hundred meters of tunnel and a lock cycle he did not have to spend. "You have got the four of them on Cadwell air until the hundredth hour," he said. "After that every one of them has to be on something, or they are on the person schedule, and I would rather come out here than have you read it off a board."

books.title: The Light at the Lava Sea
books.description: The Worlds Between Home, Book 9 of 10. Three of the Oleds are taken aboard an occupation carrier that writes everything down, while Xia climbs alone through a dark recovery trunk with a pencil and her mother's rules.
toc: A Choice No Child Should Hold
books.audience: Crossover young adult and adult readers who enjoy political science fiction, dystopian adventure, and family-centered space opera.
books.excerpt: The trunk went up at about one in four and the toy would not stay where she put it. She had him at an arm's length ahead of her, the way she had pushed him along the flat, and she got her elbows under her and came up after him, and he came back down the rake into her chin before she had made half of it. She caught him against her mouth.

books.title: The Voice at the End of Everything
books.description: The Worlds Between Home, Book 10 of 10. The concluding volume: the Directorate has broken, Aldex rebuilds authority with paper and signatures, and Xia keeps a case open against the voice that has watched eight worlds decide what to do with her family.
books.audience: Crossover young adult and adult readers who enjoy political science fiction, dystopian adventure, and family-centered space opera.
books.excerpt: The two coxswains left on the hull disagreed about whether a boat could go down, and Aldex had been listening to them disagree at the head of the boat deck for about nine minutes on the forty-fifth day when Osper Rall came up the ladder with a sheet and ended it. The older one would not fly, and he said the same three sentences every time somebody came to him. A boat goes down on a movement order. A movement order comes off the coordination desk. There is nobody on the coordination desk above clerk grade, and a clerk does not issue movement, and that is not him being difficult, that is what the word issue means.

books.title: D6 Storyteller: The Core Rulebook
books.description: The complete fiction-first tabletop roleplaying engine, with character creation, dice mechanics, a Storyteller's guide, and ten ready-to-play starter worlds spanning fantasy, sci-fi, horror, noir, superheroes, and post-apocalyptic genres.
books.audience: Seasoned Game Masters who want a light, flexible system, and new groups trying tabletop roleplaying games for the first time.
books.excerpt: There is a moment that happens at almost every game table, usually about forty minutes into the first session. Someone does something no one planned for. The group laughs, or gasps, or sits in complete silence for three seconds while everyone works out what just happened. The rules did not cause that moment. The people at the table caused that moment. The rules were just the grammar the group was using to communicate.

books.title: D6 Storyteller: High & Mythic Fantasy Companion
books.description: Ten complete high-fantasy settings for the D6 engine, each with a unique genre mechanic, ready-to-play archetypes, condition palettes, and a starter scenario.
toc: Feywild Court - Summer and Winter Solstice
books.audience: Players and Game Masters at D6 Storyteller tables who want to run campaigns in these ten worlds or use them as inspiration for their own settings.
books.excerpt: High and Mythic Fantasy represents storytelling at the boundaries of the possible. In these settings, players do not merely survive in the world; they shape its laws. Whether navigating continent-sized biomes on the corpses of deceased gods, sailing wind-ships across sky-rivers, or bonding telepathically with colossal mountain drakes, the fiction demands grand scope. The rules in this companion do not add complexity to support this weight; instead, they focus on the thematic trade-off of great power: Magic Strain, Empathy Resonance, and the blood oaths of the Fey courts. The story of high fantasy is always a story of what you are willing to give up to alter reality.

books.title: D6 Storyteller: Sci-Fi & Cosmic Frontiers Companion
books.description: Ten sci-fi settings spanning generation ships, Dyson spheres, cyberpunk megacities, and transhuman frontiers, each with its own genre mechanic and archetypes.
books.audience: Players and Game Masters at D6 Storyteller tables who want to run campaigns in these ten worlds or use them as inspiration for their own settings.
books.excerpt: The cosmic frontier is a canvas of immense scale and profound isolation. This companion takes the D6 Storyteller engine into the depths of space, where the struggle is as much against the cold physics of the universe as it is against rival factions. From the generational decay of ark ships and scrap-built cybernetic wastelands to the hyper-technological dystopias of corporate moons and Dyson spheres, these settings explore what it means to remain human in the void. Mechanics like System Fatigue, Oxygen Billing, and Precursor Artifact Resonance ensure that technology is never just background detail: it is a lifeline that can fray at any moment.

books.title: D6 Storyteller: Weird West, Piracy & Swashbuckling Companion
books.description: Ten gunpowder-and-salt-air settings covering demon-haunted frontier towns, cursed pirate seas, and swashbuckling royal courts.
toc: High Seas Piracy - Tides of Blood
Sunken Atlantis - Corsairs of the Deep
books.audience: Players and Game Masters at D6 Storyteller tables who want to run campaigns in these ten worlds or use them as inspiration for their own settings.
books.excerpt: There is a kinetic joy in swashbuckling adventure: the crash of sabers, the roar of a broadside, the quick-draw of a revolver in a dusty street. This companion focuses on settings where motion is survival and style is a weapon. You will navigate cursed seas under Aztec gold, caravan through steam-deserts, board privateer clockwork fleets, and track serpent cults in voodoo bayous. The mechanics in this book: Panache, Boarding Tension, Loa Favor, and Boiler Pressure: translate bravado directly into mechanical advantage. At these tables, playing safe is the only real failure.

books.title: D6 Storyteller: Horror, Occult & Supernatural Companion
books.description: Ten horror settings ranging from 1930s cosmic cults and slasher camps to vampire dynasties and nightmare realms.
toc: Eldritch Noir - Cult of the City
Ashen World - Dark Souls of the Ash
books.audience: Players and Game Masters at D6 Storyteller tables who want to run campaigns in these ten worlds or use them as inspiration for their own settings.
books.excerpt: Horror at the tabletop is different from horror in every other medium. The audience is not watching something happen to someone else. They are playing a character for whom something is happening, and they are doing it in a room with other people who are also playing, and all of this happens in a collaborative space that is simultaneously fictional and social.

books.title: D6 Storyteller: Cybernetics, Speculative & Alternate Tech Companion
books.description: Ten settings exploring the relationship between technology and humanity, from dieselpunk war machines and genome splicing to clockwork worlds and nanotech frontiers.
books.audience: Players and Game Masters at D6 Storyteller tables who want to run campaigns in these ten worlds or use them as inspiration for their own settings.
books.excerpt: The system may be mechanical (the diesel engine's fuel consumption, the steam boiler's pressure), biological (the genome's stability, the graft's rejection), computational (the bandwidth limit, the firewall's intrusion counter), or physical (radiation exposure, atomic charge). But the structure is always the same: the character has access to a powerful capability, that capability has a resource that depletes, and managing the relationship between the capability and the resource is the setting's primary tactical dimension.

books.title: D6 Storyteller: Superheroes, Kaiju & Anime Tropes Companion
books.description: Ten settings for caped vigilantes, mech academies, kaiju defense forces, magical guardians, and anime-inspired heroics.
books.audience: Players and Game Masters at D6 Storyteller tables who want to run campaigns in these ten worlds or use them as inspiration for their own settings.
books.excerpt: High-octane action requires mechanics that can scale from street-level vigilantism to titanic clashes that level city blocks. This companion provides the rules for running high-energy, trope-heavy anime and superhero campaigns. You will command Kaiju Defense mechs, transform into starlight magical guardians, battle in spiritual martial tournaments, patrol cyber-feudal cities as ninjas, and wield willpower energy rings. Mechanics like Titan Threat levels, Transformation clocks, Mecha Sync Ratios, and Ki Charging ensure that high-power actions feel spectacular, fast, and emotionally anchored.

books.title: D6 Storyteller: Historical & Alternate History Companion
books.description: Ten settings grounded in real history with speculative twists, from Roman legions and Sengoku Japan to WWII occult warfare and wuxia dynasties.
toc: Bronze Age Mythos - Spear of Ilium
books.audience: Players and Game Masters at D6 Storyteller tables who want to run campaigns in these ten worlds or use them as inspiration for their own settings.
books.excerpt: History is a conversation between facts and possibilities. This companion takes historical periods (Rome, the Viking age, Sengoku Japan, ancient Egypt, the American Revolution, and Imperial China) and introduces a mythic or speculative catalyst. You will fight in Roman legion formations blessed by Mars, carve Norse runes to survive Fimbulwinter, contract yokai spirits for Sengoku clan wars, and use revolutionary alchemy against British automaton redcoats. The setting mechanics, from Legion Formations and Yokai Pacts to Sun/Shadow Balance and Tabloid Fame, anchor historical drama in tactical, spiritual, and social systems.

books.title: D6 Storyteller: Quirky, Experimental & Micro-Scale Companion
books.description: Ten playful experimental settings, from tiny borrowers and living toys to arcade cabinet adventures and time-travel patrols.
toc: Miniature World - Borrowers of the Hearth
Bug World - Kingdom of the Ant
Board Game Realm - Monopoly of Empires
Card Game Summoners - Duelists of the Deck
books.audience: Players and Game Masters at D6 Storyteller tables who want to run campaigns in these ten worlds or use them as inspiration for their own settings.
books.excerpt: Tabletop gaming should occasionally challenge its own assumptions. This companion is an experimental laboratory for the D6 Storyteller system. It includes settings operating at microscopic scales (miniature household scavengers, plastic toy soldier armies, backyard bug empires, and teddy bear guardians) alongside meta-fictional structures like haunted arcade cabinets, living board game grids, ink-demon library manuscripts, card-game summoners, and temporal paradox loops. The setting mechanics, from Scale Difference and Flavor Profiles to Stuffing Integrity and Paradox Meters, reframe how approaches are applied and how scenes are won.

books.title: D6 Storyteller: Post-Apocalyptic & Speculative Worlds Companion
books.description: Ten end-of-the-world settings, from ice-age survival and sound-hunting alien horrors to the final fortress city at the end of time.
books.audience: Players and Game Masters at D6 Storyteller tables who want to run campaigns in these ten worlds or use them as inspiration for their own settings.
books.excerpt: An apocalypse is never just an ending; it is a hard reset on the relationship between humanity and nature. This companion details ten speculative post-apocalyptic settings where the landscape itself is the primary antagonist. From global ice ages and vine-travel overgrown jungles to gravity-fluctuating moon ruins, radioactive marshes, and silent cities hunted by sound-sensitive horrors, survival requires adaptability. Mechanics like Geiger Counters, Decibel meters, and Hypothermia clocks track the immediate dangers of the environment, forcing characters to adapt or be reclaimed by the ruins.
